items.referenceAnswer:
#### The client pipeline
A capture-hook (MediaStore observer) moves new items into a **pending queue** (Room table keyed by `mediaId`). A WorkManager chain, running only under `CONNECTED + unmetered` (default), processes: hash → dedupe → upload → mark done — `Capture ──> queue ──> hash/dedupe ──> resumable upload ──> mark done`. The queue is the source of truth; the UI shows 'backing up 12 of 47' from it.

#### Resumable upload
Photos are GB-scale only when videos are involved. Upload is chunked (e.g. 4 MB parts), each part acknowledged by the server, so a dead network resumes at the last ack — no restart-from-zero. Ordering: date-ascending, with newest-first optional for the 'recently added' view.

#### Deduplication
Two levels. **Client-side**: before upload, compute a perceptual hash (dhash/pHash) and a byte hash; skip if the server reports it already exists. **Server-side**: byte-level dedupe at object storage (same content → one object, many references), plus EXIF-derived checks (same timestamp + camera + size = likely duplicate). The dedupe must not block the queue — it's a fast DB lookup plus an optional server check.

#### Storage schema
Object storage (blobs) + a metadata DB. `Media { id, ownerId, takenAt, sha256, width, height, size }`. Blobs are immutable and content-addressed; mutations (edits, album adds) write new records, never mutate a blob — this makes dedupe and refs sound.

#### Organization & search
The DB is the query layer: date buckets are a projection of `takenAt`, albums are reference tables, faces come from a server-side clustering job that writes `FaceDetection` rows. Search is a separate index (OCR text + tags + face ids) built by an async pipeline; results are ranked by relevance, not file name. Search is explicitly eventual — a photo is searchable within hours, not seconds.

#### Quota & tiering
Free tier stores 'high-quality compressed' originals; paid stores originals + full res. The client respects the boundary and marks items 'only backup on paid plan'. Storage tiering: recent photos in hot tier, older in cold (archive) — a lifecycle job moves them. This keeps object costs linear instead of super-linear.

#### Battery/data budget
The WorkManager constraints are the budget: `unmetered` for video, `metered` for small photos (user opt-in), `charging` for large backlog. A daily cap on upload bytes prevents burning a monthly plan. The user sees per-item and per-session progress, and can pause per-network.

#### Failure modes
Partial upload → resumable resume. Corrupt file → requeue once then quarantine with a user notice. Deleted photo in queue → reconcile on scan. Server outage → queue holds, backoff retry (ds-0059). The queue must survive app updates and reboots (persisted + WorkManager).

#### Edits
Non-destructive: the original blob is kept, edits are stored as a small 'edit op' record; clients render original+ops. This is the Google Photos model and it makes 'restore original' trivial. The trade-off: more metadata complexity, less storage duplication.

#### Trade-offs
Content-addressed immutable blobs cost a mapping table but make dedupe and edits sound. Perceptual dedupe risks false positives at exactly the false-positive cost of a user's trust — so byte-hash first, perceptual only as a hint. Background-only upload costs freshness when the user is on metered data; that's the accepted trade-off for battery/plan sanity.

shortAnswer: Dropbox-class file sync: device files mirror to the cloud and other devices, with deltas, tombstones, and conflict detection on a flaky network.
The core is an append-only local journal as the source of truth, content-addressed chunks for block-level delta upload, and a restart-safe pull-apply-push reconcile loop.
Grading centers on conflict detection with version vectors, tombstone and garbage collection kept separate, resumable chunked upload, and convergence after long offline periods.

items.referenceAnswer:
#### The local journal
The heart: every mutation the client makes is appended to a **journal** `{ path, op, contentHash, version }` before anything else happens. The journal is the source of truth locally (like sd-0010's read-state, but richer). The UI reads the journal, not the filesystem, so 'sync state' is always consistent. On every change (a file written by another app too), the client diffs the FS against the journal and appends the delta — `FS change ──> journal append ──> reconcile (pull) ──> push delta ──> ack`.

#### Content addressing
Files are split into fixed-size chunks, each hashed; the store is content-addressed. Upload only sends chunks the server lacks. Same file on two devices = one chunk set. Block-level delta: editing a 50 MB file's last block uploads one block, not 50 MB. This is the main bandwidth win and the main complexity cost.

#### Tombstones & GC
A delete is a tombstone `{ path, op: delete, version }`, synced like any op. GC is a separate job: the server keeps a chunk while *any* live file references it; orphaned chunks are swept with a TTL. Tombstones let the delete propagate to other devices before the garbage collector runs.

#### Conflict detection
The client tags each file with a **version vector** (device → counter). When device B sees a file changed by both A and B since the last common sync, it's a conflict. Resolution: server stores both versions ('conflicted copy') and the UI shows a resolution screen once. Auto-resolution for the common case: identical content → dedupe and no conflict; pure-metadata conflict → merge metadata. The rule 'same content, no conflict' is what makes it feel magical.

#### The sync loop
A reconciler, single instance per client: pull (fetch the server journal since last cursor) → apply to local journal → diff FS → push (my new ops) → ack. Run to a fixpoint, then wait for the next event (FS change or server push). Version vectors guarantee convergence: after both sides exchange journals, both have the same logical state. On any failure the loop restarts from the last cursor — the design is *restart-safe by construction*.

#### Server model
A journal of ops per namespace + object storage for chunks. Snapshots/versioning: the journal IS the version history (each op is an edit), so 'restore yesterday' is a query, not a copy. Cross-device latency is journal-apply latency, typically seconds via push.

#### Flaky network
Chunked upload with per-chunk ack and resume; the client maintains a checkpointer so a 2 GB file resumes mid-way across sessions. Backoff with jitter on errors (ds-0059). Selective-sync folders let a quota-bound device mirror only a subset — the journal still records the whole tree, so toggling a folder on downloads the right chunks.

#### Trade-offs
Content-addressing + block deltas cost chunk plumbing but pay back on bandwidth and dedupe. Version-vector conflict detection is correct but gives the user a resolution screen that a single-file LWW would avoid — the choice is correctness vs simplicity. The journal model means every device carries the full mutation history; that's the price of restart-safe convergence.

items.referenceAnswer:
#### Delivery
MPEG-DASH/HLS with **short segments** (4–6 s) encoded at multiple bitrates (e.g. 480p → 4K). A manifest lists segments per quality. The player requests segments over HTTPS/CDN; the format decision (DASH vs HLS) is about device/DRM support, and the player abstracts both behind one API: `Manifest ──> segment fetcher ──> demux ──> decode (HW) ──> render`.

#### Adaptive bitrate
The player measures throughput from recent segment downloads (smoothed, not last-sample) and picks the highest quality that fits with headroom. Key rule: **the bitrate ladder should be sparser at the top** (the quality-per-byte gain above 1080p is tiny). Never upshift during a scene change; downshift aggressively to avoid rebuffer. The quality decision is per-segment-window, not per-segment (prevents oscillation).

#### Buffer policy
The contract: **start fast, then stay ahead.** Initial buffer: fill ~2–4 s then start playing (the 'first frame' budget drives sign-ups). After start, buffer to ~20–30 s. Underflow → pause with a buffering overlay, and pick a *lower* bitrate for the next segment to avoid recurrence. A rebuffer is the worst UX event; the policy is 'choose quality to prevent rebuffer, spend bandwidth on stability'.

#### Prefetch
During the end credits of episode N, the client preloads the first N seconds of episode N+1 (manifest + a few start segments) into the media cache. This turns 'next episode' into an instant start. The cache is bounded; prefetch is cancelled if the user navigates away.

#### Offline downloads
Explicit downloads (user picks) at a chosen quality. DRM: licenses are bound to the *device*, downloaded with a limited lifetime and checked periodically — a 30-day watch window. Downloaded content is encrypted at rest with the device key. The manifest + segments are stored in app-private storage; the player plays them through the same pipeline with `file://` sources. This shares one player code path for online/offline.

#### Resume across devices
Playback position is synced via the server every few seconds (position + segment id). On a new device, the client fetches the last position, maps it to a segment, and seeks. Clock skew and segment-boundary mapping are handled by seeking to the segment floor.

#### Analytics
The two numbers that drive everything: **startup time p95** and **rebuffer rate** (rebuffer seconds / playtime). Segment-level error rates and per-bitrate switch counts surface codec/CDN issues. All analytics are sampled and batched (never on the play path).

#### Cellular/data
On cellular, the client clamps the bitrate ladder (e.g. max 720p) unless the user opts out, and defers downloads/prefetch to WiFi. The buffer target shrinks on cellular to save data. A per-title data estimate ('this episode ~350 MB at HD') is shown pre-play.

#### Failure handling
Manifest 404 → fall back to CDN failover. Segment 404 → skip and request the next (a stutter is better than a stuck spinner), but count it. License failure → DRM-specific error with a re-request after re-auth. Network loss mid-play → pause with resume-on-reconnect at the last buffered position.

shortAnswer: A checkout and payment flow where a user is never charged twice and never told failed when it succeeded, at ~10M daily checkouts.
Idempotency first: client-generated `orderId` and per-attempt `requestId` make retry safe; one terminal success, CONFIRMED, confirmed by querying the server, never the PSP callback.
Grading hits network loss at every state with safe retries, webhook reconciliation of PENDING, tokenization shrinking PCI scope, idempotent refunds, and perfect settlement match.

Design the mobile checkout and payment flow: add a payment method, place an order, handle the network dying mid-payment, and make sure a user is never charged twice and never told 'failed' when it actually succeeded.

Assume ~10M daily checkouts, high-stakes correctness, and a fraud constraint. **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.

items.referenceAnswer:
#### Idempotency first
The client creates the order with a client-generated `orderId` (UUID) and a **request id** per payment attempt. The server is keyed on these: retrying the same request id returns the same result, never a second charge. This is the single most important rule — the entire design exists to make 'retry is always safe' true:

- `POST /orders {orderId, amount} → 200 {status: CREATED}`
- `POST /orders/{orderId}/payment {requestId, method} → PENDING`
- `GET /orders/{orderId} → CONFIRMED | FAILED`

#### State machine
`CREATED → AUTHORIZATION → PENDING → CONFIRMED` (or `FAILED → REFUNDED`). A payment has exactly **one** terminal success state (CONFIRMED) and the order screen renders only from it. The PSP gives us an `authorization` (hold) and later a `capture`; the app should treat 'authorized but not captured' as PENDING and reconcile it with the webhook. A user who sees CONFIRMED has a payment; a user who sees PENDING has an unresolved order — the UI must never blur the two.

#### The confirmation step
When the app receives 'success' from the PSP's redirect/3DS callback, it **does not** show success — it queries `GET /orders/{id}` and shows success only when the server says CONFIRMED. This one decision eliminates the 'told success but it failed' and 'told failed but it succeeded' lies. The server, in turn, only CONFIRMs after the PSP webhook verifies.

#### Network loss at each state
- Before creating the order → user just retries, nothing happened.
- After order, before payment → retry payment with the same request id — safe.
- After PSP response, before confirm query → the app shows 'processing', then polls the order status (with backoff). The server reconciles the PSP webhook and the poll converges.
- A killed app → on relaunch, the app shows the in-flight order's status from the server, not from a local guess.

#### Retry policy
Safe-to-retry: order creation, payment with same requestId (idempotent), status polling. Not-safe: capturing a PSP authorization twice — the capture step is guarded server-side by the requestId too. Timeouts: a PSP call has a strict timeout and the result is marked UNKNOWN, then resolved by webhook — never resolved by guesswork.

#### Tokenization
Card data is tokenized client-side via the PSP's SDK (never touches our servers), and we store only a token + fingerprint. PCI scope stays minimal. Fraud checks (velocity, geo, device fingerprint) run server-side at authorization; declining mid-checkout is better than declining later but the UX must be graceful.

#### Refunds
A refund is a separate operation with its own idempotent request; partial refunds are allowed and each is recorded. The dashboard shows the money movement (authorize → capture → refund) so ops can answer 'where's my money' without code.

#### Reconciliation
The daily job compares PSP settlement records vs our order DB; a mismatch (a PENDING that settled, a CONFIRMED that didn't) is paged to on-call — the money-accuracy metric is 'settlement-to-ledger match rate = 100%'. This is the correctness backstop behind every client improvement.

#### Trade-offs
The confirm-by-query step adds latency and a polling loop but kills the worst failure modes. Strict idempotency means every mutation carries an id — boilerplate but non-negotiable. You accept that a minority of payments end in 'pending' UX (better than wrong)

items.q: Design a real-time collaborative editor on mobile
shortAnswer: A Google-Docs-class mobile editor: multiple users edit one document with live presence cursors, working offline and converging on reconnect over flaky networks.
Pick a CRDT like Yjs: commutative by construction, so offline merging needs no central transform; characters carry stable ids, edits apply at frame latency.
Interviewers want the OT-versus-CRDT trade-off argued correctly, presence lossy and separate from content, concurrency-safe range-based undo, and a convergence checksum against silent divergence.
items.prompt:
Design a real-time collaborative text editor for mobile (Google-Docs-class): multiple users edit the same document with live presence cursors, working offline and converging when they reconnect.

Assume a mobile-first client with flaky networks, ~5M concurrent editors, and latency under ~1 s for a cursor to appear. **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.
items.framework: The core is **concurrency control** (CRDT vs OT), the client-server topology (presence + auth + persistence), and the mobile-specific constraints (battery, offline, keyboard latency). Run the two-phase framework; expect a debate about OT vs CRDT — know the trade-offs.

items.referenceAnswer:
#### Concurrency model — CRDT vs OT
The answer is CRDT-based (specifically a sequence CRDT like Yjs's YATA) for this scenario, and you should be able to say *why*: CRDTs are **commutative by construction** — any two users' edits applied in either order converge, which makes offline editing and reconnection trivial. OT requires a central server to transform operations and falls apart without it. The CRDT's cost is space (every character carries stable ids + tombstones) and a more complex undo — you trade space for correctness. If the interviewer pushes OT: OT wins when a single authoritative server always has the connection (low latency), CRDT wins for offline-first mobile.

#### The document model
A Yjs-like document is a **sequence of characters, each with a stable unique id** and a timestamped insert position. Deletes leave a tombstone (or are garbage-collected periodically — but GC must not break convergence). Each character carries a lamport-timestamp-ish origin so insertions between two characters are deterministic. The edit op is `insert(pos, charId, origin)` or `delete(charId)`.

#### Local latency
Local edits are applied to the local CRDT **immediately** and optimistically — the keystroke-to-character latency budget is ~16 ms (a frame), never waiting on the network. The op is queued to the outbox and synced. This is the mobile-critical part: on a phone, typing feel IS the product.

#### Sync loop and offline
The outbox is an append-only log (compare sd-0015). On reconnect, pull the server's state + push the outbox; because CRDT ops commute, merging is apply-all-ops in id order. Reconnection is a state machine: reconnect → resync state → resume presence. There is no 'conflict resolution screen' in the CRDT world — convergence is automatic; what remains is only 'whose version of the paragraph survives' (LWW per the document-level, not per character).

#### Presence
Presence is **separate from content**: a cursor = `{ userId, docVersion, position }`, ephemeral, TTL ~30 s, broadcast on a side channel (same socket, different message type). It is allowed to be eventually consistent and lossy — a dropped cursor is a non-event. Selection highlights follow the same path. Typing indicators ride on presence, not content.

#### Server
A collaboration service that keeps the document state in memory (with periodic persistence to durable storage — the write path is 'apply op → snapshot every N ops / M seconds'). The server is a **passive** applier in CRDT-land (it just applies and broadcasts), unlike OT where it transforms — which is exactly why CRDT scales out horizontally without a single-point coordination.

#### Transport
WebSocket for the live session, with exponential backoff reconnect (ds-0059) and a full resync on reconnect (cheap because docs are small text). A versioned binary protocol; ops are tiny so the wire stays lean on mobile networks.

#### Undo
Undo under concurrency is the genuinely hard part: naive per-user undo breaks. The standard approach: undo as its own op that reverts a *selection range* by inserting a new 'negative' change (the version that deletes the offending characters) rather than physically reverting. It is not always 'the thing I typed' — it is 'the state before my last change'. Accepting this is what makes concurrency-safe undo tractable.

#### Correctness metric
The scary failure is silent divergence. The metric: a **checksum of the full document state** broadcast with each sync — if two users' checksums differ for the same version, alert immediately. Convergence tests run in CI: two offline clients editing divergently, then merging, must match the oracle.

#### Trade-offs
CRDT space overhead (ids + tombstones ~2–3x text size) is the cost of offline-first correctness. Presence is engineered to be lossy so it never risks the content path. Undo is range-based, not user-history-based, which is a UX compromise the product must accept.
